blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Tactile-visual-language models combine vision and touch through a shared language space to recognize objects and materials. In real-world deployment, changes in lighting, contact quality or sensor hardware can shift visual or tactile inputs and degrade recognition performance. When both modalities contribute to a prediction, an unreliable modality can override correct evidence from the other. Since labeled data are generally unavailable during deployment, test-time adaptation offers a way to recover recognition performance from unlabeled observations. In this setting, we find that comparing accumulated observations with the text embeddings of candidate classes reveals modality reliability differences that confidence can miss. Refining features against competing classes also improves recognition beyond geometric alignment alone. These findings motivate SenseAlign, which uses a common semantic reference for test-time modality weighting and feature correction. Alignment Trust weights each modality according to its support for shared predicted classes. Anchor Realignment uses the same class text embeddings to fit a shared feature correction that separates predicted classes from alternatives. Both modules use the same unlabeled history while keeping all encoders frozen. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate strong recognition performance under both natural shifts and controlled corruptions.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Tactile–visual–language (TVL) models align visual and tactile observations
with language, bringing what a robot sees and feels into a shared semantic
space ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024a ; Feng et al., 2025 ) .
For a robot sorting materials, this connects two different views of the
same object. Touch can distinguish surfaces that look alike, while vision
reveals information beyond a small contact patch. Textual descriptions
provide a common vocabulary for these observations, allowing both senses
to contribute to recognizing objects and their physical properties.

These two views are acquired under different sensing conditions.
Poor lighting can obscure visual distinctions, while incomplete contact
or a different sensor can weaken tactile information. During recognition,
each modality scores candidate classes by comparing its representation
with their text descriptions; fusion combines these scores into a prediction.
Our analysis finds cases where equal fusion loses distinctions that one
modality still preserves, with either vision or touch taking the stronger
role. Other cases benefit from both senses. The challenge is therefore
to retain their complementarity as their relative value changes.

blocks.en:
Responding to such changes without labels is the premise of test-time
adaptation (TTA). Existing approaches learn from prediction entropy and
cross-modal information ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Niu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Guo & Jin, 2025 ) ,
including methods that address reliability bias and modality-specific
shift ( Yang et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ) .
Prediction confidence offers an intuitive signal for deciding which sense
to trust. It measures how strongly a model favors its prediction over the
alternatives, but a strong preference can persist when the prediction is
wrong. Our analysis finds precisely this mismatch: the less accurate
modality can be more confident. Giving it greater influence can reinforce
its errors. For fusion, the relevant question is whether each modality
still preserves the class distinctions needed for recognition under the
current sensing conditions.

blocks.en: 5 Related Work
blocks.zh: 5 相关工作

blocks.en:
Shared semantic representations connect contact observations with visual
and linguistic information. Image–text alignment provides a basis for
comparing visual features with class descriptions ( Radford et al., 2021 ) .
Paired visual–tactile observations establish correspondences between
appearance and contact ( Yang et al., 2022 ) , while language supervision
connects these observations with semantic descriptions ( Fu et al., 2024 ) .
UniTouch and AnyTouch extend representation learning across sensors and
modalities ( Yang et al., 2024a ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . These developments
provide the shared language space in which our adaptation operates.
We study how to use that space during deployment, when the relative
usefulness of the two sensory representations changes. In SenseAlign,
class text embeddings serve both as classification references and as
targets for comparing and correcting sensory features.

blocks.en:
Test-time adaptation learns from unlabeled observations during deployment.
TENT minimizes entropy ( Wang et al., 2021 ) ; SAR combines reliable-sample
selection with sharpness-aware optimization ( Niu et al., 2023 ) ; DeYO filters
and reweights samples using entropy and prediction changes under
perturbation ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . RoTTA uses memory and teacher–student
updates ( Yuan et al., 2023 ) . These methods derive adaptation signals
from predictions and accumulated observations, with different mechanisms
for controlling unreliable updates.
Multimodal adaptation additionally considers how updates should respond
when branches are affected differently. READ adapts
cross-modal attention ( Yang et al., 2024b ) , SuMi combines sample selection
with information sharing ( Guo & Jin, 2025 ) , and TSA routes modality-specific
adapters ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . These approaches make modality interactions
part of the adaptation problem. SenseAlign addresses their relative
contributions through a semantic comparison: it evaluates accumulated
visual and tactile observations against the same class text embeddings.
Shared observations and pseudo-label groups give this comparison a common
reference across the two modalities.

blocks.en:
Adaptation can also operate on cached features, semantic references or
contextual embeddings while keeping encoders frozen.
TDA uses a feature–pseudo-label cache ( Karmanov et al., 2024 ) ;
OGA combines Gaussian likelihoods with zero-shot priors ( Fuchs et al., 2025 ) ;
StatA uses text-derived statistical anchors ( Zanella et al., 2025 ) .
ETTA adapts contextual embeddings and prompt selection ( Dastmalchi et al., 2025 ) ;
SubTTA aligns visual and textual subspaces ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) .
MG-MTTA freezes encoders and adapts fusion using modality drift from
running anchors ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
These studies adapt how pretrained features are interpreted, including
their class associations, alignment and contributions to the final prediction.
Our TDA, OGA and StatA extensions adapt each modality separately and average
their outputs. SenseAlign couples modality weighting and feature correction
through one shared memory. Alignment Trust compares semantic support
under common class assignments, while Anchor Realignment adjusts both
modalities with a common correction. Its classification refinement
compares each assigned text embedding with competing classes, extending
the geometric alignment objective to class discrimination. This coupling
connects the choice of modality contributions with the class distinctions
preserved by the corrected features.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
SenseAlign uses one unlabeled history to compare vision and touch against
text semantics and fit a shared classification correction.
With frozen encoders, it improves recognition across natural shifts and
controlled corruptions under the evaluated protocols. Matched TAG-C
controls show that semantic weighting adds an average benefit beyond
realignment and simple confidence-based fusion. The relative benefits depend on
the backbone and sensing condition.

(b) 受评价议定书管制的腐败行为。 匹配的 TAG- C

blocks.en:

parameter-update methods (TENT, SAR, DeYO, RoTTA, SuMi), readout-adaptation
methods (TDA, OGA, StatA) and multimodal-reliability methods (READ, TSA).

maintain one state per sensor and average the two. Appendix D details the baselines and their precision qualifications. For SenseAlign we
report the two modules separately and together.

The two exceptions are consistent with Trust assigning too little weight
to vision. On UniTouch Tactile and Mixed, history-grouped margin raises
the mean visual weight from 0.709 to 0.755 and from 0.610 to 0.658,
respectively. Its net gains arise on predictions receiving more visual
weight; both panels have a more accurate corrected visual branch
(Table 22 ). Trust measures support for shared predicted
classes, which need not calibrate the relative usefulness of the corrected
branches. Its more balanced weights can therefore retain too much tactile
influence in these streams. Both fusion rules nevertheless outperform
corrected vision alone, supporting a stronger visual contribution while
retaining complementary touch. This interpretation describes the saved
weight and prediction differences; it does not establish pseudo-label
errors as their underlying cause.
